en: The *Sūtra on the Moon-Lamp Samādhi* Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Shi Xian-gong:
“Young man, there are further six kinds of triple-worlds for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six? They are as follows:”

First, the inconceivability of the three realms of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivability of the three realms of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivability of the three realms of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivability of the three realms with abiding; fifth, the inconceivability of the three realms without abiding; sixth, the inconceivability that all are empty. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of desire realm for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
What are these six?

First, the inconceivability of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) within the desire realm; second, the inconceivability of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) desire realm; third, the inconceivability of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) desire realm; fourth, the inconceivability of the abiding desire realm; fifth, the inconceivability of the non-abiding desire realm; sixth, the inconceivability of universal emptiness. These constitute the six kinds.
“Young man, furthermore,
there are six kinds of form realms for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivability of the realm of form as conditioned phenomena; second, the inconceivability of the realm of form as conditioned [existence]; third, the inconceivability of the realm of form as unconditioned; fourth, the inconceivability of the realm of form as having a dwelling place; fifth, the inconceivability of the realm of form as having no dwelling place; sixth, the inconceivability of all being empty. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of formless realms for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivability of the formless realm of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivability of the conditioned formless realm; third, the inconceivability of the unconditioned formless realm; fourth, the inconceivability of the abiding formless realm; fifth, the inconceivability of the non-abiding formless realm; sixth, the inconceivability of universal emptiness. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of practices for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivability of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivability of conditioned phenomena that are produced (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivability of conditioned phenomena that are unproduced (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivability of conditioned phenomena that abide; fifth, the inconceivability of conditioned phenomena that do not abide; sixth, the inconceivability of their universal emptiness. These are the six kinds.
“O Youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of impermanence for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is inconceivable; second, the impermanence of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; third, the impermanence of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; fourth, the impermanence of that which has abiding is inconceivable; fifth, the impermanence of that which has no abiding is inconceivable; sixth, the emptiness of all things is inconceivable. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of birth for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the arising of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is inconceivable; second, the arising of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; third, the arising of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; fourth, the arising of that which has abiding is inconceivable; fifth, the arising of that which has no abiding is inconceivable; sixth, the arising of universal emptiness is inconceivable. These are the six kinds.
"O Youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of dharmas of cessation for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are the six?

First, the inconceivable nature of the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable nature of the cessation of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable nature of the cessation of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable nature of the cessation that has a dwelling; fifth, the inconceivable nature of the cessation that has no dwelling; sixth, the inconceivable nature of universal emptiness. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of arising and ceasing for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the arising and ceasing of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is inconceivable; second, the arising and ceasing of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; third, the arising and ceasing of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; fourth, the arising and ceasing of that which has abiding is inconceivable; fifth, the arising and ceasing of that which has no abiding is inconceivable; sixth, the emptiness of all things is inconceivable. These are the six kinds.
“Young man, furthermore,
there are six kinds of cessation for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivability of the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivability of the cessation of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivability of the cessation of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivability of the cessation of that which has abiding; fifth, the inconceivability of the cessation of that which lacks abiding; sixth, the inconceivability of universal emptiness. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of tranquility for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable cessation of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable cessation of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable cessation with abiding; fifth, the inconceivable cessation without abiding; sixth, the inconceivable emptiness of all things. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of happiness for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable joy of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable joy of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable joy of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable joy of having a dwelling; fifth, the inconceivable joy of having no dwelling; sixth, the inconceivable emptiness of all things. These are the six kinds.
“Young man, furthermore,
there are six kinds of commonalities for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivability of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) in their commonality; second, the inconceivability of all conditioned things (saṃskṛta) in their commonality; third, the inconceivability of all unconditioned things (asaṃskṛta) in their commonality; fourth, the inconceivability of all that has abiding in their commonality; fifth, the inconceivability of all that is without abiding in their commonality; sixth, the inconceivability of universal emptiness (śūnyatā); these constitute the six kinds.
“O Youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of non-arising for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivability of the non-arising of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivability of the non-arising of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivability of the non-arising of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivability of the non-arising of that which has abiding; fifth, the inconceivability of the non-arising of that which has no abiding; sixth, the inconceivability of universal emptiness. These are the six kinds.
“O Youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of present [phenomena] for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are these six?

First, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are now inconceivable; second, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is now inconceivable; third, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is now inconceivable; fourth, that which has abiding is now inconceivable; fifth, that which has no abiding is now inconceivable; sixth, that all are empty is inconceivable. These are the six kinds.
“O Youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of non-extinction for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable non-extinction of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable non-extinction of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable non-extinction of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable non-extinction of that which has abiding; fifth, the inconceivable non-extinction of that which has no abiding; sixth, the inconceivable emptiness of all things. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of non-arising and non-ceasing for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivability of the non-arising and non-ceasing of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivability of the non-arising and non-ceasing of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivability of the non-arising and non-ceasing of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivability of the non-arising and non-ceasing of that which has abiding; fifth, the inconceivability of the non-arising and non-ceasing of that which has no abiding; sixth, the inconceivability of universal emptiness. These are the six kinds.
“O Youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of total emptiness for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
What are these six?

First, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are entirely empty and inconceivable; second, all conditioned things (*saṃskṛta*) are entirely empty and inconceivable; third, all unconditioned things (*asaṃskṛta*) are entirely empty and inconceivable; fourth, all that has a dwelling place is entirely empty and inconceivable; fifth, all that has no dwelling place is entirely empty and inconceivable; sixth, all are entirely empty and inconceivable. These constitute the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of emptiness for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are these six?

First, the inconceivability of the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivability of the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivability of the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivability of the emptiness of that which has a dwelling; fifth, the inconceivability of the emptiness of that which has no dwelling; sixth, the inconceivability of the emptiness of all things. These are the six kinds.
“O Youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of empty characteristics of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable mark of the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable mark of the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable mark of the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable mark of the emptiness of that which has a dwelling; fifth, the inconceivable mark of the emptiness of that which has no dwelling; sixth, the inconceivable emptiness of all things. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of empty dharmas for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are the six?

First, the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is inconceivable; second, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena is inconceivable; third, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; fourth, the emptiness of phenomena that have a dwelling place is inconceivable; fifth, the emptiness of phenomena that have no dwelling place is inconceivable; sixth, the emptiness of all things is inconceivable. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have six kinds of six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). What are these six?

First, the six sense faculties of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are inconceivable; second, the six sense faculties of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) are inconceivable; third, the six sense faculties of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are inconceivable; fourth, the six sense faculties that abide are inconceivable; fifth, the six sense faculties that do not abide are inconceivable; sixth, the fact that they are all empty is inconceivable. These constitute the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have six kinds of eye-faculties (*cakṣur-indriya*). What are these six?

First, the eye-faculty of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is inconceivable; second, the eye-faculty of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; third, the eye-faculty of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; fourth, the eye-faculty that abides is inconceivable; fifth, the eye-faculty that does not abide is inconceivable; sixth, the fact that all are empty is inconceivable. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess six kinds of ear-faculties. What are these six?

First, the ear-faculty of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is inconceivable; second, the ear-faculty of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; third, the ear-faculty of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; fourth, the ear-faculty that abides is inconceivable; fifth, the ear-faculty that does not abide is inconceivable; sixth, the ear-faculty that is entirely empty is inconceivable. These are the six kinds.
"O Youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of nose-faculties for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are these six?

First, the inconceivability of the nose-faculty of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivability of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nose-faculty; third, the inconceivability of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) nose-faculty; fourth, the inconceivability of the abiding (*sthita*) nose-faculty; fifth, the inconceivability of the non-abiding (*asthita*) nose-faculty; sixth, the inconceivability of the emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of all things. These are the six kinds.
“O Youth! Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have six kinds of tongue-faculties (*jihvendriya*). What are these six?

First, the inconceivability of the tongue-faculty of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivability of the tongue-faculty of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivability of the tongue-faculty of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivability of the tongue-faculty that abides; fifth, the inconceivability of the tongue-faculty that does not abide; sixth, the inconceivability of the emptiness of all things—these are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have six kinds of body-faculties (*kāyendriya*). What are these six?

First, the inconceivability of the body-faculty of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivability of the body-faculty of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivability of the body-faculty of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivability of the body-faculty that abides; fifth, the inconceivability of the body-faculty that does not abide; sixth, the inconceivability of the emptiness of all things—these are the six kinds.
“Young man! Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have six kinds of mental faculty (*manas-indriya*). What are the six?

First, the faculty of mind regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is inconceivable; second, the faculty of mind regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; third, the faculty of mind regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; fourth, the faculty of mind that abides is inconceivable; fifth, the faculty of mind that does not abide is inconceivable; sixth, the fact that all are empty is inconceivable. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of the six consciousnesses of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are these six?

First, the six consciousnesses of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are inconceivable; second, the six consciousnesses of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) are inconceivable; third, the six consciousnesses of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are inconceivable; fourth, the six consciousnesses that abide are inconceivable; fifth, the six consciousnesses that do not abide are inconceivable; sixth, the emptiness of all is inconceivable. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of eye-consciousness for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are these six?

First, the eye-consciousness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is inconceivable; second, the eye-consciousness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; third, the eye-consciousness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; fourth, the eye-consciousness that abides is inconceivable; fifth, the eye-consciousness that does not abide is inconceivable; sixth, the fact that all are empty is inconceivable. These are the six kinds.
"O Youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of ear-consciousness for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are these six?

First, the inconceivability of the ear-consciousness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivability of the ear-consciousness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivability of the ear-consciousness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivability of the ear-consciousness that abides; fifth, the inconceivability of the ear-consciousness that does not abide; sixth, the inconceivability of the emptiness of all things—these are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of nose-consciousness for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are these six?

First, the inconceivability of the nose-consciousness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivability of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nose-consciousness; third, the inconceivability of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) nose-consciousness; fourth, the inconceivability of the abiding (*sthita*) nose-consciousness; fifth, the inconceivability of the non-abiding (*asthita*) nose-consciousness; sixth, the inconceivability of the emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of all [these]. These are the six kinds.
“O Youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of tongue-consciousness for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are these six?

First, the inconceivability of the tongue-consciousness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivability of the tongue-consciousness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivability of the tongue-consciousness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivability of the tongue-consciousness that abides; fifth, the inconceivability of the tongue-consciousness that does not abide; sixth, the inconceivability of the emptiness of all things. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of body-consciousness for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are these six?

First, the inconceivability of the body-consciousness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivability of the body-consciousness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivability of the body-consciousness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivability of the body-consciousness that abides; fifth, the inconceivability of the body-consciousness that does not abide; sixth, the inconceivability of the emptiness of all things—these are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have six kinds of mental consciousness. What are these six?

First, the inconceivability of the consciousness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivability of the consciousness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivability of the consciousness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivability of the consciousness that abides; fifth, the inconceivability of the consciousness that does not abide; sixth, the inconceivability of universal emptiness (*śūnyatā*). These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of the six sense faculties (ṣaḍāyatana) for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are these six?

First, the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*) of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are inconceivable; second, the six sense faculties of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) are inconceivable; third, the six sense faculties of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are inconceivable; fourth, the six sense faculties that have a dwelling place are inconceivable; fifth, the six sense faculties that have no dwelling place are inconceivable; sixth, the fact that they are all empty (*śūnya*) is inconceivable. These are the six kinds.
“Young man, furthermore,
there are six kinds of visual consciousness for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivability of the eye-faculty of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivability of the eye-faculty of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivability of the eye-faculty of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivability of the eye-faculty that abides; fifth, the inconceivability of the eye-faculty that does not abide; sixth, the inconceivability of universal emptiness. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of auditory faculties for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable nature of the faculty of hearing regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable nature of the faculty of hearing regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable nature of the faculty of hearing regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable nature of the faculty of hearing regarding that which has a dwelling place; fifth, the inconceivable nature of the faculty of hearing regarding that which has no dwelling place; sixth, the inconceivable nature of the emptiness of all things—these are the six kinds.
“O Youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of olfactory consciousness for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are the six?

First, the inconceivable nature of the nose-faculty regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable nature of the nose-faculty regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable nature of the nose-faculty regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable nature of the nose-faculty regarding that which has abiding; fifth, the inconceivable nature of the nose-faculty regarding that which has no abiding; sixth, the inconceivability of universal emptiness. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of gustatory sensations for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable nature of the tongue regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable nature of the tongue regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable nature of the tongue regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable nature of the tongue regarding that which has a dwelling place; fifth, the inconceivable nature of the tongue regarding that which has no dwelling place; sixth, the inconceivability of the emptiness of all things. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of physical sensations for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are the six?

First, the inconceivability of the mental states of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivability of the mental states of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivability of the mental states of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivability of the mental states of those who abide; fifth, the inconceivability of the mental states of those who do not abide; sixth, the inconceivability that all are empty. These are the six kinds.
“O Youth! Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have six kinds of mental faculties. What are these six?

First, the mental state of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is inconceivable; second, the mental state of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; third, the mental state of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; fourth, the mental state of that which has a dwelling place is inconceivable; fifth, the mental state of that which has no dwelling place is inconceivable; sixth, the emptiness of all things is inconceivable. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have six kinds of six causes. What are these six?

First, the six causes of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are inconceivable; second, the six causes of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) are inconceivable; third, the six causes of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are inconceivable; fourth, the six causes of that which has a dwelling place are inconceivable; fifth, the six causes of that which has no dwelling place are inconceivable; sixth, the fact that all are empty is inconceivable. These are the six kinds.
"O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of activities for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable activity of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable activity of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable activity of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable activity of that which has a dwelling place; fifth, the inconceivable activity of that which has no dwelling place; sixth, the inconceivability of universal emptiness (*śūnyatā*). These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of commonalities for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivability of the commonality of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivability of the commonality of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivability of the commonality of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivability of the commonality of abiding; fifth, the inconceivability of the commonality of non-abiding; sixth, the inconceivability of universal emptiness. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of self-nature for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivability of the intrinsic nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivability of the intrinsic nature of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivability of the intrinsic nature of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivability of the intrinsic nature of that which has abiding; fifth, the inconceivability of the intrinsic nature of that which has no abiding; sixth, the inconceivability of universal emptiness. These are the six kinds.
"O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of correspondences for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable correspondence with all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable correspondence with the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable correspondence with the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable correspondence with that which has abiding; fifth, the inconceivable correspondence with that which has no abiding; sixth, the inconceivable emptiness of all things—these are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of causes of retribution for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the cause of retribution for all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is inconceivable; second, the cause of retribution for the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; third, the cause of retribution for the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; fourth, the cause of retribution for that which has abiding is inconceivable; fifth, the cause of retribution for that which lacks abiding is inconceivable; sixth, the fact that all are empty is inconceivable. These constitute the six kinds.
“O Youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of sixfold earth-tremors for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the sixfold earthquake of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is inconceivable; second, the sixfold earthquake of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; third, the sixfold earthquake of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; fourth, the sixfold earthquake of that which has abiding is inconceivable; fifth, the sixfold earthquake of that which has no abiding is inconceivable; sixth, the emptiness of all things is inconceivable. These are the six kinds.
“O Youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of eastern surging for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable eastward surging of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable eastward surging of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable eastward surging of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable eastward surging of that which has abiding; fifth, the inconceivable eastward surging of that which has no abiding; sixth, the inconceivable emptiness of all things—these are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of setting in the west for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the setting sun of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is inconceivable; second, the setting sun of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; third, the setting sun of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; fourth, the setting sun of that which has abiding is inconceivable; fifth, the setting sun of that which has no abiding is inconceivable; sixth, the emptiness of all things is inconceivable. These are the six kinds.
“O Youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of southern surges for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable southern surging of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable southern surging of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable southern surging of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable southern surging of that which has abiding; fifth, the inconceivable southern surging of that which has no abiding; sixth, the inconceivable emptiness of all things. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of northern disappearance for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable northern disappearance of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable northern disappearance of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable northern disappearance of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable northern disappearance of that which has abiding; fifth, the inconceivable northern disappearance of that which has no abiding; sixth, the inconceivable emptiness of all things. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of surging toward the limit for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable leaping beyond the limits of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable leaping beyond the limits of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable leaping beyond the limits of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable leaping beyond the limits of abiding; fifth, the inconceivable leaping beyond the limits of non-abiding; sixth, the inconceivable emptiness of all things. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of passing away in the intermediate state for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable submergence within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable submergence within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable submergence within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable submergence within that which has a dwelling; fifth, the inconceivable submergence within that which has no dwelling; sixth, the inconceivable [submergence] wherein all are empty. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of ignorance for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the ignorance of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is inconceivable; second, the ignorance of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; third, the ignorance of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; fourth, the ignorance of that which has a dwelling place is inconceivable; fifth, the ignorance of that which has no dwelling place is inconceivable; sixth, the emptiness of all things is inconceivable. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of conditioned activities for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivability of conditioned phenomena as conditions for conditioned phenomena; second, the inconceivability of conditioned phenomena as conditions for the unconditioned; third, the inconceivability of unconditioned phenomena as conditions for conditioned phenomena; fourth, the inconceivability of conditioned phenomena with abiding as conditions; fifth, the inconceivability of conditioned phenomena without abiding as conditions; sixth, the inconceivability that all are empty—these are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of conditioned activities regarding form for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are these six?

First, the inconceivability of the form conditioned by the practice of all formations; second, the inconceivability of the form conditioned by conditioned formations; third, the inconceivability of the form conditioned by unconditioned formations; fourth, the inconceivability of the form conditioned by formations with abiding; fifth, the inconceivability of the form conditioned by formations without abiding; sixth, the inconceivability that all are empty—these are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of conditions for form for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable conditions of conditioned form; second, the inconceivable conditions of conditioned form; third, the inconceivable conditions of unconditioned form; fourth, the inconceivable conditions of abiding form; fifth, the inconceivable conditions of non-abiding form; sixth, the inconceivable emptiness of all things—these are the six kinds.
“O Youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of name-and-form for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivability of the name-and-form of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivability of the name-and-form of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivability of the name-and-form of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivability of the name-and-form that has a dwelling; fifth, the inconceivability of the name-and-form that has no dwelling; sixth, the inconceivability of their total emptiness. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, there are six kinds of name-and-form conditioned by the six sense bases. What are these six?

First, the inconceivability of the six sense bases conditioned by the name-and-form of all formations (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivability of the six sense bases conditioned by the name-and-form of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivability of the six sense bases conditioned by the name-and-form of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivability of the six sense bases conditioned by the name-and-form that has abiding; fifth, the inconceivability of the six sense bases conditioned by the name-and-form that lacks abiding; sixth, the inconceivability of their universal emptiness. These are the six kinds.
"O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of contact conditioned by the six sense bases for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivability of contact conditioned by the six sense bases of all formations (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivability of contact conditioned by the six sense bases of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivability of contact conditioned by the six sense bases of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivability of contact conditioned by the six sense bases that have a dwelling place; fifth, the inconceivability of contact conditioned by the six sense bases that have no dwelling place; sixth, the inconceivability of their universal emptiness. These are the six kinds.
"O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of feeling conditioned by contact for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are these six?

First, the inconceivability of sensation conditioned by contact with all formations (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivability of sensation conditioned by contact with the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivability of sensation conditioned by contact with the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivability of sensation conditioned by contact with that which has a dwelling place; fifth, the inconceivability of sensation conditioned by contact with that which has no dwelling place; sixth, the inconceivability of the emptiness of all things—these are the six kinds.
“Young man, furthermore,
there are six kinds of craving conditioned by sensation for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivability of craving conditioned by feeling regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivability of craving conditioned by feeling regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivability of craving conditioned by feeling regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivability of craving conditioned by feeling regarding that which has a basis (*sapratiṣṭhita*); fifth, the inconceivability of craving conditioned by feeling regarding that which is without a basis (*apratiṣṭhita*); sixth, the inconceivability of the emptiness of all these; these constitute the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of grasping conditioned by craving for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable grasping conditioned by craving for all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable grasping conditioned by craving for the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable grasping conditioned by craving for the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable grasping conditioned by craving for that which has a dwelling place; fifth, the inconceivable grasping conditioned by craving for that which has no dwelling place; sixth, the inconceivable [grasping] wherein all are empty. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of existence conditioned by grasping for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are these six?

First, the inconceivability of the existence conditioned by the grasping of all formations (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivability of the existence conditioned by the grasping of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivability of the existence conditioned by the grasping of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivability of the existence conditioned by the grasping of that which has abiding; fifth, the inconceivability of the existence conditioned by the grasping of that which has no abiding; sixth, the inconceivability of the emptiness of all these. These are the six kinds.
“O Youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of birth with conditions for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable dependent origination of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable dependent origination of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable dependent origination of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable dependent origination of that which has a dwelling; fifth, the inconceivable dependent origination of that which has no dwelling; sixth, the inconceivable emptiness of all things. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of conditions for birth that lead to old age and death for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivability of old age and death as having conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as their condition for arising; second, the inconceivability of old age and death as having the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) as their condition for arising; third, the inconceivability of old age and death as having the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as their condition for arising; fourth, the inconceivability of old age and death as having that which has abiding (*sthiti*) as their condition for arising; fifth, the inconceivability of old age and death as having that which lacks abiding (*asthiti*) as their condition for arising; sixth, the inconceivability of all being empty (*śūnya*); these are the six kinds.
“O Youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of the extinction of ignorance for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable cessation of ignorance regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable cessation of ignorance regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable cessation of ignorance regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable cessation of ignorance regarding that which has a basis; fifth, the inconceivable cessation of ignorance regarding that which has no basis; sixth, the inconceivable emptiness of all things—these are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of cessation of practice for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable cessation of the formations of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable cessation of the formations of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable cessation of the formations of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable cessation of the formations of those who abide in existence; fifth, the inconceivable cessation of the formations of those who do not abide in existence; sixth, the inconceivable emptiness of all things—these are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of the cessation of form for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable cessation of the form of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable cessation of the form of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable cessation of the form of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable cessation of the form that abides; fifth, the inconceivable cessation of the form that does not abide; sixth, the inconceivable emptiness of all things. These are the six kinds.
"O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of the cessation of name-and-form for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable cessation of conditioned name-and-form; second, the inconceivable cessation of conditioned name-and-form; third, the inconceivable cessation of unconditioned name-and-form; fourth, the inconceivable cessation of abiding name-and-form; fifth, the inconceivable cessation of non-abiding name-and-form; sixth, the inconceivable emptiness of all—these are the six kinds.
"O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of the cessation of the six sense bases for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable cessation of the six sense bases of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable cessation of the six sense bases of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable cessation of the six sense bases of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable cessation of the six sense bases that have a dwelling; fifth, the inconceivable cessation of the six sense bases that have no dwelling; sixth, the inconceivable emptiness of them all. These are the six kinds.
“O Youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of the cessation of contact for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable cessation of contact with all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable cessation of contact with the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable cessation of contact with the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable cessation of contact with that which has abiding; fifth, the inconceivable cessation of contact with that which has no abiding; sixth, the inconceivable emptiness of all things—these are the six kinds.
“O Youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of the cessation of craving for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable extinction of craving for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable extinction of craving for the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable extinction of craving for the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable extinction of craving for abiding; fifth, the inconceivable extinction of craving for non-abiding; sixth, the inconceivable emptiness of all things—these are the six kinds.
"O Youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of cessation through grasping for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable cessation of the grasping at all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable cessation of the grasping at the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable cessation of the grasping at the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable cessation of the grasping at that which has a dwelling; fifth, the inconceivable cessation of the grasping at that which has no dwelling; sixth, the inconceivable emptiness of all things—these are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of arising and ceasing for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the arising and ceasing of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is inconceivable; second, the arising and ceasing of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; third, the arising and ceasing of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; fourth, the arising and ceasing of that which has abiding is inconceivable; fifth, the arising and ceasing of that which has no abiding is inconceivable; sixth, the emptiness of all things is inconceivable. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of the cessation of old age and death for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable cessation of old age and death regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable cessation of old age and death regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable cessation of old age and death regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable cessation of old age and death regarding that which has abiding; fifth, the inconceivable cessation of old age and death regarding that which has no abiding; sixth, the inconceivable emptiness of all things. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of the extinction of sorrow and lamentation for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable cessation of the sorrows of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable cessation of the sorrows of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable cessation of the sorrows of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable cessation of the sorrows of that which has a dwelling; fifth, the inconceivable cessation of the sorrows of that which has no dwelling; sixth, the inconceivable emptiness of all things—these are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivability of the four truths of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivability of the four truths of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivability of the four truths of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivability of the four truths of that which has abiding; fifth, the inconceivability of the four truths of that which has no abiding; sixth, the inconceivability of universal emptiness. These constitute the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of the truth of origination for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the truth of the accumulation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is inconceivable; second, the truth of the accumulation of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; third, the truth of the accumulation of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; fourth, the truth of the accumulation of that which has abiding is inconceivable; fifth, the truth of the accumulation of that which has no abiding is inconceivable; sixth, the fact that all are empty is inconceivable. These are the six kinds.
“Young man, furthermore,
there are six kinds of the truth of cessation for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the truth of cessation regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is inconceivable; second, the truth of cessation regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; third, the truth of cessation regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; fourth, the truth of cessation with abiding is inconceivable; fifth, the truth of cessation without abiding is inconceivable; sixth, the emptiness of all things is inconceivable. These are the six kinds.
“O Youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of causes of suffering for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the cause of suffering in all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is inconceivable; second, the cause of suffering in the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; third, the cause of suffering in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; fourth, the cause of suffering in that which has abiding is inconceivable; fifth, the cause of suffering in that which lacks abiding is inconceivable; sixth, the fact that all are empty is inconceivable. These are the six kinds.
“O Youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of causes for the accumulation [of merit] for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the cause for the accumulation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is inconceivable; second, the cause for the accumulation of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; third, the cause for the accumulation of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; fourth, the cause for the accumulation of that which has abiding is inconceivable; fifth, the cause for the accumulation of that which is without abiding is inconceivable; sixth, the fact that all are empty is inconceivable. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of causes for cessation for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the cause for the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is inconceivable; second, the cause for the cessation of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; third, the cause for the cessation of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is inconceivable; fourth, the cause for the cessation of that which has abiding is inconceivable; fifth, the cause for the cessation of that which lacks abiding is inconceivable; sixth, the fact that all are empty is inconceivable. These are the six kinds.
“O Youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of causes for the path of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are these six?

First, the causes for all paths of practice are inconceivable; second, the causes for conditioned paths are inconceivable; third, the causes for unconditioned paths are inconceivable; fourth, the causes for abiding paths are inconceivable; fifth, the causes for non-abiding paths are inconceivable; sixth, the fact that all are empty is inconceivable. These constitute the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of conditions for suffering for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable conditions for the suffering of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*); second, the inconceivable conditions for the suffering of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-duḥkha*); third, the inconceivable conditions for the suffering of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-duḥkha*); fourth, the inconceivable conditions for the suffering of abiding; fifth, the inconceivable conditions for the suffering of non-abiding; sixth, the inconceivability that all are empty. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of accumulation of conditions for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable conditions for the accumulation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable conditions for the accumulation of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable conditions for the accumulation of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable conditions for the accumulation of that which has abiding; fifth, the inconceivable conditions for the accumulation of that which has no abiding; sixth, the inconceivability of universal emptiness. These constitute the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of cessation of conditions for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable conditions for the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable conditions for the cessation of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable conditions for the cessation of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable conditions for the cessation of that which has a dwelling; fifth, the inconceivable conditions for the cessation of that which has no dwelling; sixth, the inconceivable emptiness of all things—these are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of objective conditions for the path of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable conditions for the path of all practices; second, the inconceivable conditions for the conditioned path; third, the inconceivable conditions for the unconditioned path; fourth, the inconceivable conditions for the path with abiding; fifth, the inconceivable conditions for the path without abiding; sixth, the inconceivability of universal emptiness. These constitute the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of ascetic practices for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable ascetic practice of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable ascetic practice of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable ascetic practice of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable ascetic practice with abiding; fifth, the inconceivable ascetic practice without abiding; sixth, the inconceivable [realization that] all are empty. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of accumulative practices for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable accumulation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable accumulation of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable accumulation of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable accumulation of that which has abiding; fifth, the inconceivable accumulation of that which has no abiding; sixth, the inconceivable emptiness of all things. These are the six kinds.
"O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of practices for cessation for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable extinction of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable extinction of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable extinction of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable extinction with abiding; fifth, the inconceivable extinction without abiding; sixth, the inconceivable emptiness of all things—these are the six kinds.
“Young man, furthermore,
there are six kinds of bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices of the path. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable practice of the path of all phenomena; second, the inconceivable practice of the conditioned path; third, the inconceivable practice of the unconditioned path; fourth, the inconceivable practice of the path with abiding; fifth, the inconceivable practice of the path without abiding; sixth, the inconceivable emptiness of all things. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have six kinds of consciousness of suffering. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable consciousness of the suffering of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*); second, the inconceivable consciousness of the suffering of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-duḥkha*); third, the inconceivable consciousness of the suffering of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-duḥkha*); fourth, the inconceivable consciousness of abiding suffering; fifth, the inconceivable consciousness of non-abiding suffering; sixth, the inconceivability that all are empty. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of the accumulation of consciousness for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable accumulation of consciousness regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable accumulation of consciousness regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable accumulation of consciousness regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable accumulation of consciousness regarding that which has abiding; fifth, the inconceivable accumulation of consciousness regarding that which has no abiding; sixth, the inconceivability of the emptiness of all things—these are the six kinds.
"O Youth! Furthermore, there are six kinds of the cessation of consciousness for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are these six?

First, the inconceivable consciousness of the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable consciousness of the cessation of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); third, the inconceivable consciousness of the cessation of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); fourth, the inconceivable consciousness of the cessation with abiding; fifth, the inconceivable consciousness of the cessation without abiding; sixth, the inconceivability that all are empty. These are the six kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess six kinds of consciousness of the path.
What are these six?

First, the inconceivable consciousness of the path of all practices; second, the inconceivable consciousness of the conditioned path; third, the inconceivable consciousness of the unconditioned path; fourth, the inconceivable consciousness of the abiding path; fifth, the inconceivable consciousness of the non-abiding path; sixth, the inconceivable consciousness of universal emptiness. These are the six kinds.

“O Youth! All the conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*) of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas—whether conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), with abiding or without abiding—are empty; these are the six fundamental practices as fully explained above. If one were to explain them through extensive metaphors, they would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon.”

Regarding the *Candrapradīpa-samādhi-sūtra* spoken by the Buddha: this is the version known as the *Candrapradīpa-samādhi-sūtra* within the Song edition of the Tripiṭaka. Although it was translated by an earlier official, its textual phrasing and meaning differ significantly from those of the Derge (Tangut) edition of the Tripiṭaka; it remains unknown which of the two is correct.
According to the *Kaiyuan lu*, a note beneath the title of the translation by my late father states:
"Also titled *The Scripture on the Ten Deeds of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva*," and regarding its length, it specifies: "ten sheets."
I have now examined it, and it is indeed that *Danzang* (Cinnabar Treasury) scripture.

In this region, the *Songzang* (Song Dynasty Canon), from the *Sanjie* (Three Realms) through to the *Daoshi* (Realization of the Way)—spanning approximately ninety sections in total—expounds all matters using the six modes of exposition; there has never been a single mention of "ten matters."
Furthermore, regarding its length—being twenty sheets of ancient paper—it is evident that it was not translated by Master Xian.

I fear that the Song Canon may have lost the translation of Master Xian, while instead preserving what was lost from the ancient editions: a translation by An Shigao that lacks a named translator. Seeing the title *Candrapradīpa-sūtra* in the catalog, which was indeed translated by Master Xian, one realizes that the name has been erroneously attributed.
Furthermore, the Record states:

"Extracted from the seventh fascicle of the Great Sūtra. Upon current inspection, it appears to be from the latter half of the fifth fascicle; why it does not yet correspond exactly remains to be further verified.
